entries.content:
I’m still on hiatus from online life, but I am returning for a moment to paste in the massage you see below, which was meant for my Buy Me a Coffee subscribers before I deleted that account. This old blog seems the best place for it. And indeed, it’s possible that when I end my sabbatical I will end up writing here after all: I still despise the WordPress interface and am profoundly annoyed by the “security measures” taken by Reclaim Hosting that prevents me from using MarsEdit as my blogging app, but my old system of posting longer pieces here and quotes-&-links at micro.blog was a pretty good system, and I may habe to resurrect it in some form.

I’ve always had two tracks as a writer. On the one hand, I do my scholarly work within my particular field, which is essentially writers, artists, and intellectuals of the mid-twentieth century, especially but not only Christians, with a sideline in the movies and music of that era. And then the rest of my writing (blogging and the essays) covers a pretty wide range of topics, but at any given time there’s typically one major theme that I’m pursuing.

Throughout the 2010s, the dominant subject of my writing was attention. I was troubled by the ways that our digital environment — which was becoming all-encompassing at that time with the rise of the smartphone — was making it impossible for us to attend to anything properly. we struggled (as we still struggle) to read and think well. So that was my topic, in many essays and two trade books.

Then, towards the end of that decade, I began to think a lot about the ways in which our continuously distracted, agitated, stimulated state was keeping us mindlessly reactive to today’s social media kerfuffles — whatever the Two Minutes’ Hate of that particular day happened to be. That got me thinking about the possibility that attending to the past was a way of breaking the repeating cycles of outrage. My idea was that encountering people from the past, in ways that let us see with equal clarity how they are like us and unlike us, is a kind of training in dealing with our neighbors. If we can learn to be charitable toward people from the past, then maybe that can be a kind of training in neighborliness. That’s actually is an idea that goes back very far for me: I make a first step in articulating it in my Theology of Reading book, which came out a quarter-century ago. But the concept gets developed most fully in Breaking Bread with the Dead, where I argue that the encounter with the past is a way of breaking the hold of tribalism and replacing that tribalism with a renewed humanism, an awareness of what all human beings have in common, as a way of breaking down the alienation, the hostility, the repugnance that we feel toward those who are not part of our tribe. And that basic theme gets articulated in several recent essays about possible anchors for a renewed humanism.

But another thing that I found myself thinking about at the same time is: What is first theology? Where should the articulation of Christian theology begin? I thought that perhaps an awareness of our common humanity might be a first step toward a Christian theological anthropology. But then, increasingly, as my comments about humanism fell on deaf ears, I began to think that you might need at least some elementary theology in place before you can acknowledge the bonds that we all share as human beings.

(One other possible first theology I wrote about in detail really only once, though it’s something I think about all the time. That is suspicion: suspicion of the corruptions of the human order, the kind of suspicion that some people think of as paranoia and other people think of as mere realism. And the great apostle of suspicion is Thomas Pynchon.)

But very recently, my thoughts have been turning in a different direction. Basically, I’ve been thinking that we all need to get out more. That is, our thinking about ourselves and about the world is overly dominated by our response to the things that human beings make. We are dominated by technology. I mean that in the sense that we consider everything in light of its technological aspect — politics, ethics, the arts, everything — but also we’re continually experiencing the good earth itself through the mediation of our technologies. This has become especially clear to me as we’re going through this period of compulsive writing and thinking and feeling about AI.

I first really saw this coming when I wrote an essay about what I called the Standard Critique of Technology: What happens if we all agree that the SCT is correct, but we haven’t really solved any of our problems? That question has really been preying on my mind. And the question has come to a point in a certain way with my upcoming retirement, because one of the chief things that Teri and I want to do in our retirement is to see more of the beauties of Creation. To spend more time in America’s protected areas of wilderness, really explore those, and see the world that God has made, not the things that human beings have made. Direct, unmediated experience of Creation — that’s what we find ourselves longing for.

So, in preparation for all that, I’ve been reading extensively in what we might call American conservationist writing, or nature writing. For instance, I’ve been reading Douglas Brinkley’s three-volume history of the role that American Presidents have played in promoting ecological awareness and in actually saving landscapes and waterscapes from depredation. As I’ve been thinking about these movements, I’ve reflected that it’s truly a shame that Christians have by and large ignored these issues. Almost all the people who have done the most to shape our sensitivity to the world we live in were not in any sense orthodox Christians, though many of them clearly had a theology — it was just a theology that began and ended with the idea of God as creator. (See John Muir.)

It seems to me that I was already beginning to head in this direction, not just when I was writing about the limits of the SCT, but when I was connecting that to Daoism. There is a contemplation of the ten thousand things that is characteristic of Taoism, and I feel it ought to be incorporated somehow, transformed Christocentrically, into a Christian’s understanding of creation.

Now I’m ready to think considerably more deeply about these things. Some writings that are proving exceptionally helpful to me right now are the letters of Gary Snyder and Wendell Berry — and also the poetry of both men. Berry called them “distant neighbors,” and the distance was both geographical and metaphysical — but the neighborliness was real, and powerful and meaningful, to them both. They’re giving me a great deal to think about. And I’ll eventually give an account of my thoughts, though I don’t yet know where, when, or how.

Ciao for now.
